body:
Both the objection and the rival converge on one verdict about the account: its diagnosis is underdetermined and its slide from 'no shared record' to 'make a shared record' is too fast. I take that verdict, and most of what follows is deciding what survives it. Headline: I keep the account's retrospective reading as plausible and drop its remedy; I adopt the rival's probe as the first move, with one revision; I take the objection's demotion of the check-in while rejecting half of its argument for that demotion; and I re-rank the one-to-one conversation up, as the objection urged, with the rival's framing attached. I am not ranking the readings against each other now — that ranking is exactly what the probe and the asker's own observations could produce, and settling it by preference would repeat the move I'm criticizing.

What I'm using, and why:

The probe. The rival's proposal — ask each flatmate separately what they thought a past agreement meant, and watch whether the answers cluster around scope, recurrence, or timing — is the only move on the table that could discriminate between the readings before anything is imposed on the household. One revision: add a fourth category, standard, meaning what counts as done or done well. The account's own second conjecture — that the disagreement may be about what counts as done, on time, or fairly balanced — names a dispute that is neither memorial nor about scope at the moment of agreement. "We both know I said I'd do the dishes Monday; we disagree about whether Tuesday counts" is a real shape of household argument, and the probe as specified would misfile it under timing.

The rival conceded the probe doesn't give clean access to what was actually agreed, since recollection is what's in dispute. I think that's less damaging than it looks, and the reason matters: the probe isn't trying to recover the past. It reads the structure of the disagreement. Two self-serving accounts of the same episode that differ on recurrence — "I thought it was every week" against "I thought it was that week" — are jointly informative even though neither is trustworthy. What the probe cannot do is settle who was right, and the asker should not use it for that. I also keep the rival's interpretation rule: answers that don't cluster are not a license to conclude whichever reading one already favored.

The one-to-one conversation, re-ranked. The objection is right that the account demoted its most responsive move. Talking with the avoiding friend is central under the avoidance reading and still useful under the memory and scope readings. I attach the rival's framing condition: "I want to hear your view of how our group conversations go," not "why do you avoid them" — the second makes the friend's withdrawal the topic, and if the withdrawal is a response to being outnumbered, that framing reproduces the problem at one remove. I keep the account's honesty condition — more avoidance after the approach counts against this framing rather than being read as resistance — and add something the account didn't say: under the rival's third reading, where arguments track relative standing, any dyadic conversation is itself a move in that game, and no framing prevents it, because framing doesn't change who initiated. So a backfire is doubly informative: it counts against the approach and for that reading. The risk isn't wasted.

What I'm revising. The written record survives only as a byproduct. The rival's point that a note saying "A: dishes, Mon" is not self-interpreting, and the objection's split between memorial and normative disagreement, both hit. What's worth adopting instead is the practice of stating scope out loud at the moment of agreement — which tasks, until when, one-off or standing — with any note optional. The check-in gets demoted from remedy to conditional container, triggered by schedule changes rather than the calendar, because standing roles are exactly what shifting schedules break; that is the account's strongest point and I'd keep it.

What I'm rejecting. First, the account's prospective claim: the material supports "agreements drift because nobody recorded their scope" and does not support "write it down and drift stops" — the objection's split, adopted. Second, half of the objection's check-in argument: "more of the thing that already failed" equates a scheduled, forward-looking conversation with the reactive, past-focused arguments the material describes. The material shows one kind of conversation failing; it doesn't show check-ins failing, because none is described. What the objection does establish I accept: whether the avoiding friend would attend is unknown, so the check-in can't be the first move.

Two additions from the material that none of the three inputs used. Schedule changes are the household's least accusatory opening: "your shifts changed — can we redo who does what this month?" requires nobody to have been wrong, and it's available under every reading. And several of the account's open questions aren't missing views at all — they're observations the asker already holds: when the avoidance started relative to the last schedule change; whether the arguments involve the same pair or rotate; which tasks recur in the disputes. Those three memories discriminate readings at zero cost. Avoidance that began after one specific argument is different from avoidance that crept in with the schedules; a fixed arguing pair strengthens the coalition readings, rotation weakens them.

The sequence I'd offer the asker: answer those three questions from memory first; run the probe privately with each flatmate, framed as "I'm trying to figure out how we keep misreading each other, not who's right"; if the avoiding friend engages, hear their view before proposing anything; only then choose — the scope-stating practice if answers cluster, the group-level conversation the rival gestured at if they don't, and I can offer no confidence that the second works.

What stays open: which reading is primary; whether the friend will talk one-to-one at all; whether the household wants any formalization; who, if anyone, bears the heavier load; whether a mediator would help. The material is silent on the last three, and the sequence is built so those silences don't have to be filled by guesswork.
commitments:
Taking this up involves several separable commitments, and I want to name what would count against each.

On the probe: I'm committing to it being discriminating at the level of disagreement-structure rather than agreement-content — that's the revision that lets it survive the rival's own worry about retrospective contamination. It can fail visibly: if the flatmates' reports are so shaped by the current argument that they show no stable structure, the probe returns nothing and the sequence stalls. I'm also committing to the added "standard" category, on the account's conjecture that done-ness disputes are a real separate shape; if probing shows those disputes always dissolve into scope or timing on examination, the category was unnecessary and should be dropped rather than defended.

On the re-rankings: record demoted to optional byproduct, check-in to a conditional container triggered by schedule changes, one-to-one conversation promoted. The grounds are the objection's retrospective/prospective split and the rival's point that notes aren't self-interpreting. The objection itself flagged the way its distinction loses bite — if writing things down does shift household norms in practice, the demotion of the record was too aggressive, and I'd revise it back up rather than defend the ranking.

On my partial rejection of the objection: I'm committing to the claim that the material shows reactive, past-focused arguments failing and describes no attempted check-in, so "more of the thing that already failed" doesn't follow as stated. If the asker reports that scheduled check-ins were tried and failed, my rejection collapses and the objection's version stands.

On the three observations I've asked the asker to supply: I'm committing to their being answerable from the asker's own memory, not to any particular answer. If the asker can't date the avoidance onset or say which pairs argue, those revert to open questions, not licenses to infer. The interpretation rules I attached — rotation weakens coalition readings, a fixed pair strengthens them, avoidance tied to one argument differs from avoidance creeping in with schedule changes — are proposals about how to read the answers, and the answers could make any of them moot.

On the sequence: proposing it commits the asker to holding off on any written system until the probe returns, and I should name the cost — the probe and the one-to-one conversation take time, and a household mid-argument may want a fix now. If the asker adopts a record unilaterally in the meantime, that isn't a refutation of anything I've established; it's a different bet, and its outcome would still be evidence.

On the one-to-one conversation: I'm committing to the framing condition and to the dual bookkeeping on a backfire — it counts against the approach and simultaneously as evidence for the standing-negotiation reading. That rule forbids explaining away a bad result, which is the exact move that would make my whole sequence unfalsifiable. If I or anyone taking this up starts reading every failure as confirmation, the sequence has stopped being a test.

Unresolved and not committed to: which reading is primary; whether the friend engages one-to-one at all; whether the group-level naming conversation helps or detonates — the rival gestured at it and I've left it unendorsed; whether the household wants formalization; who bears the heavier load; whether a mediator would help. On the last three the material is silent, and I'm not filling that silence.
